title: In topology optimisation the gradient is the whole advantage, and the density picture shows why
summary: Two figures from one study: a convergence plot with a final bar chart, and the material layouts the three methods ended with. Together they show that a method that can use an exact gradient finds a structure, while methods that only see scores are still close to grey noise at the same cost.

media.alt: Two panels. Left: compliance on a log axis from about 150 to 700 against evaluation batch or iteration from 0 to 150. A blue gradient curve falls steeply to about 140 and flattens; short red and green curves for a genetic algorithm and reinforcement learning cover only the first few iterations near 600. Right: bar chart on a log axis of final compliance, gradient 143.7, genetic algorithm 593.3, reinforcement learning 577.1.

source.caption: Gradient descent beats a genetic algorithm and reinforcement learning by ~4x, at equal evaluation budget
group: 16_16_topopt_gradient_vs_heuristics: convergence curves (150 evaluations, 288 design variables) and the final-compliance bar chart for the three methods (representative)
17_17_topopt_density_fields: the three material layouts side by side, gradient, genetic algorithm and reinforcement learning, each labelled with its compliance
source.note: The project text says the same SIMP problem, budget of about 150 evaluations and constraint projection were used for all three; the genetic algorithm used roughly double the evaluation budget. One run per method is drawn.

read_the_figure.question: At equal cost, which method finds the stiffest structure, and what does the layout look like when it has actually learned the load path?
read_the_figure.axes: Left panel: x is evaluation batch or iteration (0 to 150), y is compliance on a log axis, lower is stiffer. Right panel: one bar per method of final compliance, log axis. Second figure: three small images of a 24 by 12 grid of cells, grey level = material density from white (void) to black (solid).
look_at: The blue curve falls by about a factor of five in the first 30 iterations and then flattens. A flat tail means convergence, not a stuck run, if the layout is crisp.
The red and green curves are very short: they end near the 8th batch on the x axis. The x axis counts batches, not function evaluations, so the three curves do not use the axis in the same way.
In the bar chart, read the printed numbers. On a log axis bar lengths do not show the ratio.
In the layouts, the gradient result has crisp black members and white voids with a clear truss; the other two are speckle: mostly grey cells with no continuous load path.
Grey cells are intermediate densities: not yet a physical solid-or-void design.
read_the_figure.proves: That, for this one problem and one run per method, the method with an exact gradient is far ahead at this cost, and that the layout agrees with the compliance numbers. It does not prove that the other methods cannot get there with a much larger budget.
if_wrong: A crisp-looking layout with a high compliance: the result is a poor local optimum or the volume constraint is wrong.
A low compliance with a layout full of grey: the structure relies on intermediate densities that cannot be manufactured.
A heuristic that looks similar to the gradient result: check that the constraint handling was identical.
must_check: The same problem, mesh, loads, volume fraction and constraint handling for every arm.
The cost axis is the same quantity for every curve (here the left axis is batches, not evaluations).
Several seeds for the stochastic arms; a single run is drawn.
Material layouts are shown beside their compliance number, as here.
Compliance is on a log axis, which is stated.
as_drawn: Printed final compliance: gradient 143.7, genetic algorithm 593.3, reinforcement learning 577.1. Ratios (computed): 593.3 / 143.7 = 4.13 and 577.1 / 143.7 = 4.02, so about four times.
The initial compliance of all three is near 600 to 700 (read by eye), so the heuristics improved only slightly from it, by about 5 to 15 percent, while the gradient arm reduced it to about a fifth.
The mesh looks like 24 by 12 cells, consistent with the 288 design variables in the title (24 x 12 = 288).
The compliance of the vine mark in the project's logo (10.916) is from a different problem and is not comparable with these numbers.

terms.meaning: Solid Isotropic Material with Penalisation: each cell has a density between 0 and 1, and its stiffness is the density raised to a power, so intermediate densities are inefficient and the optimiser is pushed to black or white.
Work done by the load on the structure, force times displacement. Minimising it maximises stiffness for the given load.
A cap on the total material, which stops the trivial answer of filling everything with solid.
A fixed-point update that scales each density by the ratio of its sensitivity to a Lagrange multiplier chosen so that the volume holds.
The derivative of compliance with respect to one cell's density. It is cheap here because the compliance problem is self-adjoint.
A population method that evolves designs by selection, crossover and mutation, using scores only.
A policy-gradient learner that draws designs from a probability distribution and shifts it towards higher reward, again using scores only.
Intermediate densities. They are a numerical device, not buildable material.

remember: Compliance is a stiffness measure: lower is stiffer.
A self-adjoint problem gives all 288 sensitivities from the one solve already done.
Heuristics that see only scores must search 288 dimensions blindly; the gradient gives a direction in all 288 at once.
Compare cost with a stated, shared unit: iterations, batches and evaluations are different things.
A layout and its number belong together: crisp layout with a low number, or neither is trusted.

understand.title: Why a gradient helps so much here
understand.text: The design has 288 variables. A score-only method must discover by trial how each cell affects the result, while the gradient reports that effect for every cell at once from one extra vector operation. At a budget of about 150 evaluations the score-only methods have barely begun to sample the space.

understand.title: Why the layouts look the way they do
understand.text: The gradient arm moves each cell towards the load path and, through the penalisation, towards black or white, so a truss emerges. The heuristics move random cells and keep the better ones, which at this budget leaves a speckled field.

steps.title: The optimisation problem
steps.tex: \min_{\boldsymbol\rho}\ c(\boldsymbol\rho)=\mathbf F^{\mathsf T}\mathbf u\quad\text{s.t.}\quad \mathbf K(\boldsymbol\rho)\,\mathbf u=\mathbf F,\ \ \sum_e v_e\rho_e\le V,\ \ 0<\rho_{\mathrm{min}}\le\rho_e\le1
steps.note: The equilibrium equation Ku = F ties displacement to the design, and the stiffness matrix K is assembled from cell stiffnesses that depend on density.

steps.title: SIMP stiffness law
steps.note: Raising density to p makes half-density material give much less than half the stiffness, so the optimiser prefers solid or void. The exponent used in the project is not stated on the figure.

steps.title: The exact sensitivity
steps.note: Because the objective is F transpose u with the same F that drives the equilibrium, the adjoint equals the displacement itself: self-adjoint. The sensitivity needs no extra linear solve. It is negative: adding material always lowers compliance.

steps.title: Volume-preserving update (optimality criteria)
steps.note: Cells whose sensitivity is above the multiplier gain material, the others lose it. The multiplier is found by bisection. The damping exponent and move limits are implementation choices.

steps.title: Ratio of final compliances
steps.note: Computed from the printed values: a factor of about four. The ratio is not read from the log-scale bars.

worked.title: How much did each arm improve from the start?
worked.problem: Take the starting compliance as about 650 (read by eye from the left panel) and use the printed final values 143.7, 593.3 and 577.1. What fraction of the start does each retain?

solution.text: Divide each final value by the start.

worked.answer: The gradient arm keeps about 22 percent of the starting compliance; the heuristics keep about 90 percent. The starting value is an eyeball reading, so those fractions are approximate to a few points.

analyze.q: The left panel's x axis is 'evaluation batch / iteration' and the GA and RL curves are about eight units long, while the caption says equal budget. What is the likely meaning, and what does it imply for how to compare the curves?
analyze.hint: One iteration for a population method is many evaluations.

analyze.q: The two heuristic layouts are mostly grey. What does that say about their compliance values, and about whether those designs could be built?
What could make the gradient arm look worse than it should: name two experimental choices.
analyze.hint: Filter radius, move limits, initial density.

evaluate.q: Is this a fair verdict on 'heuristics versus gradients' in general? State which parts of the claim the evidence supports.
evaluate.hint: One problem, one run, one budget, 288 variables.

evaluate.q: If the budget were ten thousand evaluations, what would you expect the red and green bars to do, and what would you do to check?
evaluate.hint: Repeat the study at several budgets.

create: Redraw the left panel with cumulative function evaluations on the x axis for all three arms, so that costs line up, and add a band over several seeds for GA and RL.
Design a variant of the study where the gradient is unavailable (for example a black-box simulator) and say which methods you would compare.

checks.q: What does compliance measure in this study?
checks.answer: The structure's flexibility under the load: work done by the load. Lower compliance means a stiffer structure.

checks.q: Final compliances are 143.7 and 593.3. By what factor is the second larger?
Why is the sensitivity of compliance with respect to density negative?
checks.hint: Adding material in a stiffness problem.
checks.answer: Adding material can only stiffen the structure under a fixed load, so compliance falls. The expression has a minus sign and a non-negative energy term, so it is never positive.

checks.q: Why should a layout be shown next to every compliance number?
checks.hint: A number can come from an unbuildable design.
checks.answer: Because compliance alone cannot reveal grey, speckled or disconnected material. The layout shows whether the number comes from a believable load path.

checks.q: How would you make the comparison fair to a population method?
checks.answer: Plot best compliance against cumulative function evaluations for every method, give each the same total, and run several seeds.
